Lewd. Priests on duty were not even allowed to approach to their wives, and the most pure women had no right to go into the interior of the temple. (Calmet) And. Greek, "in the courts, and also bringing in improper things." (Haydock)

Jew. None did this except he were legally questioned. It would have unnecessarily brought on a persecution. (Haydock) --- The very name was become criminal, as that of Christian was afterwards. (Calmet)

Sacrifices. Greek, "each month, to the sacrifice (and feast) of entrails," (Haydock) which were given back to him who presented the victim. (Grotius) --- The eastern kings celebrated their birth-days; Epiphanes did it every month, 1 Machabees i. 61., and Matthew xiv. 6. --- About. Greek, "to follow the march;" pompeuein. (Calmet) --- Protestants, "to go in procession to Bacchus, carrying ivy." Ward (Err. p. 114) reads pompaduein, and refers the reader to the lexicon to see if there be any thing in it like the Catholic processions, or whether it signify so much as "to go about," as other Protestant Bibles translate it. These interpreters frequently use Catholic terms, where they might render them odious. (Id.[Ward, Err. p. 114.?]) (Haydock)

Ptolemeans, who resided at Ptolemais. (Calmet) --- Most Greek copies have Ptolemee, chap. iv. 45. (Haydock) --- We find that many of the neighbouring nations invaded the Jews, but were repressed by Judas, 1 Machabees v. 15.

Women. See 1 Machabees i. 64., &c. (Calmet) --- Besides the former massacres, (chap. v.) four great martyrdoms are here recorded: first, of two women, with their children; second, of others keeping the sabbath; third, of Eleazar, ninety years old; and fourthly, of the seven brethren, with their mother, chap. vii. (Worthington)
Philip, the governor of Jerusalem. (Challoner) --- Chap. v. 22. (Haydock) --- See 1 Machabees ii. 31. (Calmet)
Now. A necessary caution for the weak in times of persecution. (Worthington) --- See chap. vii. 32., and Judith viii. 22., and 1 Machabees ii. 52.
Punished, lest they should become incorrigible. When God neglects to do this, his anger is most terrible, Ezechiel xvi. 42. (Calmet)

Sins. God seems at present to take no notice of the crimes of the Gentiles, or he exterminates them at once, as he did the Chanaanites, Sodom, &c. But the Jews he corrects for their amendment and trial. The sages of paganism never inculcated such excellent maxims.

Scribes; a priest. (St. Ambrose) --- He suffered at Antioch, before the king, chap. vii. 1. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] l. 2.) --- The Fathers highly extol his fortitude and virtue, styling him the father of the seven brothers, and the protomartyr of the old law. (Calmet) --- Yet we find others unnamed suffering before him, ver. 10. (Haydock) --- Eleazar was learned in the Scriptures, and in all divine and human knowledge. (Worthington)

Hateful. Greek, "criminal life, and went first of his own accord to be bastinaded;" tumpanizesthai. (Haydock) --- St. Paul probably alluded to this torment, Hebrews xi. 35. It was used among the Jews. (Calmet, Diss.)

Life. He would not eat swine's flesh to save it. Greek, "But spitting it out, (as those ought to come forward who expect to be tortured; or avenged. amunesthai) of which things it is not lawful to taste through love of life." (Haydock)

Wicked pity. Their pity was wicked, in as much as it suggested that wicked proposal of saving his life by dissimulation. (Challoner) --- To feign or make outward shew of consenting to a false religion, is never lawful. (Worthington) --- Greek, "They were set over that wicked feast or sacrifice," splagchnismo, (Haydock) in which the entrails were eaten. (Calmet) --- In this sense the term is used [in] ver. 7 and 8 by the Vulgate. Here Pity is preferred, as the man seemed to be actuated by it. (Haydock) --- This generous martyr would not scandalize the weak, by doing a thing in itself lawful, which would have been deemed a prevarication. He was guided by those excellent maxims which Christ, St. Paul, and St. Saba (Mart. Ap. xii.) have inculcated and practised, Matthew xviii. 7., and Romans xiv. 14., and 1 Corinthians viii. 4, 10. (Calmet)

The other. Literally, "hell," or the grave. (Haydock) --- Under the old law the saints could not enter heaven, but at their departure were detained in limbo. (Worthington) --- Some holy doctors have declared that they would rather go to hell than commit a sin. (St. Anselm) --- They understand by hell the torments of that place, but not the opposition to God's will, which is found in the damned, and constitutes one of the greatest of their pains. (Haydock)
Age. "Old age ought to be the haven, not the shipwreck, of a former life." (St. Ambrose, de Jacob.) (Worthington)

Dead. Nothing could be more express for the torments after death. As the time of the Messias drew near, these truths were more developed, chap. vii. 9., and Wisdom v. 16., and Psalm i. 6. (Calmet) (Grotius) (Matthew xii. 32.)
Pains. Some of the martyrs seem not to have felt their torments. God made them suffer no more than they could bear. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on 2 Maccabees

But not long after, the king sent a certain old man from Antioch, who was to compel the Jews to depart from their ancestral ways and the laws of God, etc.

These same events are reported in the preceding book, namely that Antiochus, through his messengers, defiled the temple by setting up in it the idol of desolation upon the altar of God; and we have given the allegorical interpretation of that passage there.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Nor did anyone simply confess that he was a Jew. They were, however, led under bitter coercion on the king's birthday to the sacrifices, etc.

They said that the Gentiles acknowledged Liber Pater as the lord of wine, whose rites Antiochus ordered to be especially celebrated on his own birthday, because he believed that this god favored his birthday. For they wish Liber to be named from libera mens ("free mind"), because, as it were, males in intercourse are freed by his benevolence when their seeds are discharged; on account of this the same Liber is depicted with a womanly and delicate body. For they say that women are assigned to him, and wine, for the arousing of lust. Therefore also his brow is encircled with a vine-leaf, but with his head having been formed, he has a vine crown and a horn, because when wine is drunk in Greek fashion [sparingly] and in moderation, it brings joy, but when beyond measure, it stirs up quarrels and, as it were, gives horns. He is also called Lyaeus from the drink called lyaeum, because with much wine the limbs are loosened. This same god is in Greek called Dionysus from Mount Nysa, where he is said to have been raised. Moreover, there is also a city Nysa in which the same Liber is worshipped, where he is called Nisaean. The rites of Liber Pater were first introduced among the Greeks by Orpheus, and he was the first to celebrate them on a mountain of Boeotia and at Thebes, where Liber was born, close by. Because he frequently resounded with the song of the cithara, he was called Cithaeron; and the rites are now called Orphic, in which he himself was torn to pieces, and afterwards also captured, almost at the same time as Faunus. But which of them came first in age can be doubted, since in those same years Latinus and Priam reigned. Likewise their fathers were Picus and Laomedon, during whose reign Orpheus, with the Argonauts, reached the shore of the Athenians.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Therefore Eleazar, one of the foremost scribes, a man advanced in age, etc.

This Eleazar, whom the wickedness of Antiochus, a most cruel king, forced in his old age to eat pork, represents the Christian people, whom the savagery of Antichrist will attempt, before the end of the world, to turn to idolatry and to the filthiness of life. Moreover, Eleazar is interpreted as "My God is my helper," a name that most fittingly applies to the people of the faithful, who, together with the Psalmist, know how to say to the Lord: "You are my helper; do not forsake me" (Ps. 27:9); and again, "My deliverer, my God, I will hope in him" (Ps. 18:2). But just as the brutality of the wicked king was unable to compel Eleazar to eat pork, so neither will the cruelty of Antichrist be able in any way to defile the company of the elect with any uncleanness.

n: Scourges, made of leather thongs; taureis. (Haydock) --- These brethren are styled Machabees; as Judas rendered this name so famous, that all who suffered or fought valiantly for religion in those times, went by this appellation. Josephus has much embellished this history, and Erasmus still more. The tombs of these martyrs were shewn at Antioch. (Calmet) --- Their names are not known. (Haydock) --- Those who wish to see more, may consult the large discourse of Josephus on the Machabees, (Worthington) though this work be contested, and St. Cyprian iv. ep. 6; St. Ambrose i. of. 40.; St. Chrysostom; St. Augustine; St. Leo, &c. (Worthington)

Pleasure. Literally, "be comforted," as the Septuagint translate, (Haydock) Deuteronomy xxxii. 36. It may imply that God will avenge or chastise his servants, and then restore them to favour. This latter sense is here adopted, ver. 35.

Language. The Jews have always been very attentive to their own language, though they be forced to learn others for the sake of commerce, and to hold conversation with those among whom they live. This young man, no doubt, understood Greek, in which language his brother had probably spoken. The mother addressed her children in the Hebrew or Syriac tongue, ver. 21, 27. (Calmet)

Most wicked. The martyrs have sometimes been inspired by God to speak in harsh language to magistrates; though their office generally commands respect. (Haydock) --- Life. The resurrection is clearly specified in all these answers. The Redeemer was near at hand. (Calmet) --- Christiani fuerunt....factis. (St. Augustine, ser. i. 2.)
Power. Nothing could be more free than this answer, which greatly resembles that of Christ, John xix. 11. (Calmet)
Seven. The last was not yet dead: but he was before this was written, so that the mother's praise was perfect. (Haydock)
Womb. This has always astonished the learned, the infant being formed often against the woman's desire, Job x. 10., and Wisdom vii. 2. (St. Augustine, anima i. 15.) (Calmet)

Despising. Literally, "despising the voice of the insulter." Greek, "fearing or perceiving that the speech was reproachful." (Haydock) --- Syriac, "turned aside not to hear the reproaches," &c. He did not understand Hebrew; but perceiving the constancy of the young men, he thought that their mother exhorted them to refuse compliance. (Calmet) --- Happy. This is beyond the power of riches or of any king. (Haydock)

Promised. A promise regards something good; so that if a person should even bind himself by an oath to do evil, he must refrain, as to comply would he another sin. (Worthington) --- This woman promised to counsel, but not as the king wished, (Haydock) to gain a prolongation of life and worldly honours for her son. (Menochius) --- Such an equivocation was lawful. (Worthington) --- The king might blame himself if he was deceived. (Haydock)

Three years. So long physicians judged it best for children to suck, till they could take solid meat. (Vales. lxxxiii.) (Genesis xxi. 8.) (Calmet) --- "Chrysippus assigns three years for the nurse." (Quint. i. 1.)
Nothing, not out of pre-existent and eternal matter. (St. Augustine, Nat. boni xxvi.) (Romans iv. 17.) --- So God can reduce all to nothing, chap. viii. 18.
Mercy, in eternity of bliss, ver. 23. (Syriac) (Calmet)
Life. Greek, "short labour of eternal life, are fallen under the covenant of God." (Haydock) --- They enjoy that life which God promised.
God. This was accomplished, ver. 17., and chap. ix. 15.
Cease. The persecution was severe, but short. Judas the next year (the year [of the world] 3838.; Calmet) began to liberate the nation, (Haydock) by God's mercy, chap. viii. 5, 27.

Undefiled, by idolatry. We read [in] 4 Machabees that he threw himself into a boiling cauldron; (Calmet) and Josephus says his mother "jumped into the fire that she might not be touched by any." But this is uncertain. The Church honours St. Apollonia, who acted thus; (Feb.[February?] ix.) it is supposed by divine inspiration. (Haydock)

Consumed. Greek, "died" (Haydock) of joy: (Sixth. Bib. v. Victoria) she placed herself amid the dead bodies, and begged of God to release her soul; which was granted. (Arabic) (Grotius) --- But most believe that she suffered martyrdom immediately after her children. (Josephus, &c.) --- The Church honoured these martyrs from the earliest ages, and before any other of the Old Testament. We may justly style them the martyrs of the resurrection, as none at that time had spoken of it so distinctly. Sts. Naz.[Gregory of Nazianzus?], Max. of Turin, Gaudentius, &c., have pronounced panegyrics upon them.
Sacrifices. Greek splagchnismous, chap. vi. 21. (Haydock) --- Read 1 Machabees ii. 1., where the wars begun by Mathathias, and persecuted by Judas, are recorded. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on 2 Maccabees

What is indicated by this mother of seven sons, if not the fruitfulness of Mother Church, who through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit brings forth for God the Father adopted sons? The cruelty of typical Antiochus, that is, of Antichrist, although it tears apart through its ministers the offspring of the fathers, and through himself both them and their mother with various torments, nevertheless is in no way able to draw them into blasphemy. But what reward awaits this woman and her sons in the future for the suffering they have endured in the present, Isaiah shows, saying: Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; sing praise and hymn, you who were not bearing: because the deserted woman has many sons, more than she who has a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles, do not spare: make your cords long, and strengthen your pegs. To the right and to the left you will break forth, and your seed will inherit nations. Do not fear, for you shall not be confused nor put to shame. For you shall not be ashamed, because you will forget the confusion of your youth, and you will no longer remember the criticism of your widowhood. For he who made you will rule over you, the Lord of hosts is his name, and your redeemer is the Holy One of Israel: he shall be called the God of all the earth, because the Lord has called you like a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and like a wife rejected from youth, says your God. For a brief moment I have forsaken you, but with great mercies I will gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while, but with everlasting mercy I have had pity on you, says the Lord your redeemer. Poor little one, storm-tossed, without any comfort. Behold, I will lay your stones in order, and I will found you upon sapphires. And I will set jasper as your battlements, and your gates in carved stones, and all your borders in desirable stones: all your children taught by the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children. And you shall be founded in righteousness. Stay far from oppression (Isa. 54:1-7). But the fact that after the sons the mother too was put to death shows that, after the triumphs of each of the sons of the Church, by which they overcame their enemies, they will enter with free souls into eternal rest. Finally, Mother Church herself, the mother of all the faithful, will be brought to completion at the end of the world, and, taking the trophy of glory over all her enemies, will possess the everlasting kingdom.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

However, how the most blessed martyr and most gentle doctor Cyprian (On the Exhortation to Martyrdom 11), writing about these same seven brothers to Fortunatus, would discourse upon them in eloquent speech after the manner of speakers, we have judged should be inserted in this place; and among other things he says therefore: "But what, in the Maccabees, do the seven brothers, alike in the lot both of birth and of virtues, signify, except the number seven fulfilled in the sacrament of perfect completion? For therefore the seven brothers, united in martyrdom, are as at the beginning there were, in the divine ordering, seven days containing seven thousand years; as the seven spirits and the seven angels who stand and minister before the face of the Lord; and the seven-branched lampstand in the tabernacle of witness; and in the Apocalypse the seven golden lampstands (Rev. 1:20); and in Solomon the seven pillars on which Wisdom built her house (Prov. 9:1). So also here the number of the seven brothers, by its quantity embracing the number of the seven Churches, is in accord with what we read in the first book of Kings (1 Sam. 2:5), that the barren woman bore seven. And in Isaiah seven women seize upon one man, whose name they beg to be called upon them (Isa. 4:1). And the apostle Paul, who remembers this legitimate and fixed number, writes to seven Churches. And in the Apocalypse (Rev. 1) the Lord directs His divine commands and heavenly precepts to seven Churches and to their angels; and this number is now found here in the brothers, so that the legitimate completion may be fulfilled. With the seven children the mother also is clearly joined, as their source and root; she who afterwards bore the seven Churches, she herself first and single, founded upon the rock by the word of the Lord. Nor is it without meaning that in the sufferings the mother alone is with her children; for the martyrs, who in their passion bear witness that they are sons of God, are now reckoned as having no Father but God alone, just as in the Gospel the Lord teaches, saying: 'Call no man your father upon the earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven' (Matt. 23:9)."
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

How illustrious, moreover, how great were the proclamations of confession which they uttered, what great evidences of faith they provided! King Antiochus, hostile, indeed, in Antiochus the Antichrist was foreshadowed, sought to stain the glorious mouths of the martyrs, joined and invincible in the spirit of confession, with the defilement of swine's flesh; and when he had severely beaten them with scourges and had been able to achieve nothing, he ordered pans to be heated. When these were red-hot and blazing, he commanded that the one who had spoken first, and who by the loyalty of his courage and faith had the more provoked the king's wrath, be brought to them and fried, after first stretching out and cutting off the tongue which had confessed God. This happened to the martyr in a more glorious way; for the tongue that had confessed the name of God ought itself to go first to God.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Next, against the second he created more cruel punishments; and before he tortured the other members, he flayed off the skin of his head with the hair, in deliberate hatred. For since the head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God, he who was crushing the head in the martyr was persecuting God and Christ in the head. But he, trusting in his martyrdom and promising himself the reward of the resurrection from the recompense of God, cried out and said: "You indeed, powerless one, destroy us from this present life; but the King of the world will raise us who die for His laws to the eternal resurrection of life."
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

The third, when his tongue was demanded, promptly put it out; for from his brother he had already learned to despise the punishment of cutting out the tongue. He also steadfastly stretched forth his hands to be cut off, greatly blessed in this kind of punishment, to whom it befell, with hands extended for suffering, to imitate the likeness of the Lord's passion.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Likewise the fourth, despising the tortures with equal courage and answering the king with a heavenly voice to confound him, cried out and said: "It is better, being given over to death by men, to look for the hope from God, to be raised again by Him to eternal life; for you shall have no resurrection to life."
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

The fifth, besides the fact that by the strength of his faith he trampled underfoot the king's butchery and cruel and manifold torments, was also, inspired by the spirit of divinity to foreknowledge and understanding of things to come, a prophet to the king of the indignation of God and of the vengeance that would swiftly follow: "Having power among men," he says, "though you are mortal, you do what you will. But do not suppose that our race has been forsaken by God. Only wait, and you will see His great power, how He will torture you and your seed." What a relief that was to the martyr, how great, how immense a consolation in his torments, not to think of his own sufferings, but to proclaim the punishments of his torturer!
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

In the sixth, moreover, not only his courage, but also his humility must be proclaimed; that the martyr claimed nothing for himself, nor puffed up the honor of his confession with proud words, but attributed to his own sins the fact that he suffered persecution from the king, while he ascribed it to God that he would afterwards be avenged. He taught that martyrs are modest, that they trust in vengeance being taken, and that they boast of nothing in their passion. "Do not," he says, "deceive yourself in vain; for we suffer these things for our own sakes, in that we have sinned against our God. But do not think that you will remain unpunished, who have set yourself to fight against God."
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Admirable also was the mother, who, neither broken by the weakness of her sex nor shaken by manifold bereavement, looked with willing eyes upon her dying children, and reckoned those sufferings of her offspring not as pains but as glories, offering to God as great a martyrdom by the courage of her eyes as her sons offered by the torments and suffering of their limbs.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

When six had been killed and punished and one of the brothers still remained, the king promised him riches, power, and many things, so that his cruelty and savagery might be soothed by the consolation of having at least one subdued, and he asked that the mother should plead with him to yield about the son. She did indeed plead with her son, but as was fitting for the mother of martyrs, as was fitting for one mindful of the Law and of God, as was fitting for a woman who loved her sons not delicately but courageously. For she pleaded, but that he might confess the Lord; she pleaded that her son might not be separated from his brothers in the fellowship of praise and glory; counting herself then the mother of seven sons, if it should fall to her lot to have borne seven sons to God, not to the world.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Arming him therefore and strengthening him, and in that moment bringing forth her son by a happier birth, she said: "My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, and gave you milk for three years, and nourished you, and brought you to this age. I beg you, my son, look upon heaven and earth; and seeing all that is in them, understand that God made them out of nothing, as well as the race of men. Therefore, my son, do not fear this executioner, but, proving yourself worthy of your brothers, accept death, so that in that mercy I may receive you together with your brothers." Great is the praise of the mother in her call to courage, but greater still in the fear of God and in the truth of faith, in that she promised nothing for herself or for her son from the honor of the six martyrs, nor did she believe that the plea of the brothers would be of any avail for the salvation of one who denied; instead she persuaded him rather to become a sharer in their passion, so that on the day of judgment he might be found together with his brothers. After these things the mother also dies with her children; for nothing else was now fitting, since she who had borne and made martyrs should be joined with them in the fellowship of glory, and that she herself should follow those whom she had sent on before to God.

n: Towns. Literally, "castles." Greek, "villages." It also means a town or village; and at this time, Judas chiefly dwelt in the deserts. (Haydock) --- Many particulars of this war are found [in] 1 Machabees iii. (Calmet)
Lord. Prayer is particularly requisite before battle. (Worthington)
Blood of the Jews unjustly slain. (Menochius) --- The voice of Abel's and of Christ's blood is very different, Genesis iv. 10., and Hebrews xii. 24.

Philip seeing, &c. The governor of Jerusalem found himself unable to contend with Judas, especially after the victories he had obtained over Apollonius and Seron, 1 Machabees iii. (Challoner) --- He was left two years before (Calmet) to afflict the Jews. (Worthington)

Twenty thousand. The whole number of the forces sent at that time into Judea, was 40,000 footmen and 7,000 horsemen; (1 Machabees iii. 30.) but only 20,000 are here taken notice of, because there were no more with Nicanor at that time of the battle. (Challoner)

Talents. So much the king was in arrear, owing to his prodigality. For which reason he was gone beyond the Euphrates [River] to raise money. His father had to pay the Romans 15,000 talents in twelve years.
Ninety. Often (Calmet) a talent was paid for one slave. (Josephus, Antiquities xii. 4.)
Justice. Greek diken, "vengeance" (Haydock) against the enemies. (Calmet)
Covenant. A just and religious cause is the best help in war. (Worthington)

Seven thousand. In the Greek it is six thousand. But then three thousand of them had no arms, 1 Machabees iv. 6. (Challoner) --- If the army was divided into four companies of 1,500, there would be only 6,000. But if Judas had with him 3,000, it would consist of 7,500. (Calmet) --- Reconciled. Greek, "consternated at," &c. (Haydock)

Galatians. That is, the Gauls, who having ravaged Italy and Greece, poured themselves in upon Asia in immense multitudes, where also they founded the kingdom of Galatia, or Gallo-Græcia. (Challoner) --- This battle is nowhere else recorded in Scripture. But it seems to allude to the aid given to Soter by the Jews, (Worthington) when he repulsed the Galatians. (Appian.) --- Antiochus the great rewarded them for their valour shewn in behalf of his father. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] xii. 3.) (Worthington) --- Six. Greek, 8,000. --- When. Greek, "with 4,000 Macedonians; when the Macedonians being at a stand, the 6,000 (Grabe substitutes 8,000) slew twelve myriads," &c. (Haydock) --- Historians have not specified this irruption, as it had no farther consequences. The Galatians were very powerful under Antiochus the great, and sided with him. The consul, Manlius, made them promise to keep within their own territories. But they did not observe this agreement, since they attacked Eumenes while Epiphanes persecuted the Jews. It is not agreed when they made the invasion of Babylonia, then defended by Jewish and Macedonian troops under the king of Syria.
Joseph; perhaps the same with John Gaddis, or simply a relation.

Esdras. Greek and Syriac, "Eleazar;" probably the brother of Judas. Grotius thinks that the latter read the account of the death of Eleazar, which must be understood of the martyr, (chap. v.) as the brother of Judas was slain under Eupator. Perhaps the law regarding people going to fight was read; (Deuteronomy xx. 6., and 1 Machabees iii. 56.) or as Judas prepared for battle by prayer and fasting, some portions of Scripture might be selected while they were at Maspha. --- Help. So he specifies the victory of God, chap. xiii. 15. (Calmet)
Above nine thousand, viz., including the three thousand slain in the pursuit. (Challoner) --- Three thousand fell on the field of battle, 1 Machabees iv. 15.
Time. They wished to be in the camp before the sabbath, having designed to collect the spoils.
Widows. Judas follows the spirit rather than the letter of the law, Numbers xxxi. 27., and Deuteronomy xiv. 29.

Timotheus. Chap. x. 24. The particulars of this war are not given. It seems to have taken place after the temple was purified, ver. 31. We must distinguish this first war from another mentioned, chap. x. 24., and 1 Machabees v. 5. Judas defeated another Timotheus beyond the Jordan [River], chap. xii. 10., and 1 Machabees v. 11, 34, 37.
Jerusalem. They had taken all but the citadel, chap. x. 1.

Apparel, as a general. (Calmet) --- Fleeing. Greek, "like a fugitive, having rendered himself destitute, he came through the midland country to Antioch above all being fortunate himself in," &c. (Haydock) --- He was too happy in having escaped. The Roman edition and Syriac agree with us, "being very unhappy," &c., (Calmet) which is substituted by Grabe. (Haydock)

f: Commentary on 2 Maccabees

And the things which the history of the former book relates about Mattathias, the father of Maccabeus, and his brothers, the writer of this present book, striving also for brevity, has omitted, and turned himself to recounting the deeds of Judas and his battles, narrating some of them but, according to his manner, omitting very many. But because we have already, for the most part, set out the allegory of this above, we do not think it necessary to repeat what has been said once. If anyone should ask what the six thousand men, who were joined to Judas at the beginning, signify, let him recognize that, through the perfection of the numbers six and one thousand, the perfect sincerity of the soldiers of Christ in faith is indicated, their devotion being complete. Therefore, in the Acts of the Apostles, it is written to the Jews about the primitive Church: "Now the multitude of believers were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things which he possessed was his own, but they had all things in common. And with great power the apostles gave their testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord, and great grace was upon them all" (Acts 4:32-33).
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

In the previous book it is written that Antiochus, when about to set out for Persia, left within the kingdom Lysias, a noble man of royal lineage, in charge of the royal affairs and to bring up Antiochus his son; and that this same Lysias chose Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, and Nicanor, and Gorgias, powerful men from among the king's friends, and sent them with forty thousand men to destroy the Jews according to the king's command. Now, however, it is reported that Philip wrote to Ptolemy the general that he should bring assistance to the king's affairs, and that he sent Nicanor for this purpose, giving him twenty thousand armed men, and appointing Gorgias, a military man, to join him. For this Philip, on his return from Persia to Babylon, the aforesaid King Antiochus set over his whole kingdom and gave him the crown, and the robe, and the ring, so that he should bring up Antiochus his son, and nurture him, and reign; but this same Philip, when the aforementioned Lysias together with the younger Antiochus was returning to Antioch, they found ruling over the city and attacked him. Therefore the question arises, how Philip can be said to arrange through Ptolemy the march of Nicanor and Gorgias to Judea, whereas the earlier narrative relates that, while the elder Antiochus was staying in Persia, that same Nicanor together with Gorgias as general, and Lysias as organizer, were overcome and put to flight by the Jews, and that this became known to Antiochus on his return, and that on account of this he fell into sickness out of grief, because it had not been done to the Jews as he had intended. This, unless I am mistaken, is resolved in no other way than that Philip, when the empire had been entrusted to him, wrote the same decree to the generals of Syria to be carried out, which Lysias had already previously undertaken to attempt to carry out, but had not completed, nor was he able to achieve it among the Jews in the way he had planned by his own expedition, as the following history shows.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

This was briefly mentioned in the previous book: namely, that merchants gathered with gold and silver to buy the sons of Israel as slaves for themselves. But here it is recounted more clearly that, by Nicanor, who promised the king to make up the tribute owed to the Romans from Jewish slaves, the merchants themselves were invited to purchase Jewish slaves.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

Concerning this coming of Nicanor into Judea, which took place under Antiochus, the former book clearly does not speak; yet, while relating that he was chosen by Lysias together with Ptolemy and Gorgias, powerful men, with an accompanying mass of followers, to invade and lay waste Judea, it asserts that under Demetrius he was sent there and wished by deceit to seize and invade Judea; but he was not able to prevail. Now it has already been said above that Nicanor himself bears the figure of hypocrites, who do everything in a pretended manner. But Judas engages in battle against Nicanor and his allies with seven thousand men and defeats them, because through the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, the people of the Church together with their leaders conquer all their enemies; nor does any Jew, or pagan, or heretic, or schismatic, or any hypocrite or wicked man ever win victory over it. Rather, he himself, together with his victorious King, will possess the trophy of glory forever.
Commentary on 2 Maccabees

In place of "victory songs" I have read in another edition "days of victory." Therefore, with the enemies overcome, Judas celebrates the feast, because together with the saints each person, through the grace of Christ, triumphs over the ancient enemy, and, filled with spiritual joy, ought to compose fitting praises and render many thanks to his maker; nor is it proper for someone to become ungrateful who remembers that he has been helped by divine work.

n: At. Read 1 Machabees iv. 28. (Worthington) --- Time. The year [of the world] 3840. The motives and ill success of this journey are given [in] 1 Machabees iii. 31., and vi. 1. (Calmet)

Persepolis; otherwise called Elymais, (Challoner) a chief (Worthington) "city of Persia." Hence Elymais may be called Persepolis. (Haydock) --- The famous city of this name, where Cyrus had built a palace to the astonishment of the world, had been (Calmet) burnt by Alexander when intoxicated, and urged on by a harlot. (Curtius v. 15.) --- Noble ruins still remain on the Araxes.
Ecbatana, capital of Media. (Calmet) --- See chap. i. 16. (Haydock)
Forward. He felt a violent fit of the cholic.
Man. He seems to have claimed divine honours, ver. 12., and chap. v. 21., and ix. 8., and Daniel xi. 36. (Arabic) (Calmet)

Not like. Because his repentance was not for the offence committed against God, but barely on account of his present sufferings. (Challoner) --- For these he really grieved, 1 Machabees vi. 11. Yet was not sorry for the offence against God and men. So the damned acknowledge that their punishments are inflicted on account of their sins, yet have not true repentance. (Worthington) --- In like manner Esau repented for the loss of his birthright, Hebrews xii. 17. (Menochius) --- Epiphanes had abandoned God, who now laughs at him, (Proverbs i. 26.) as some of the Machabees had threatened, chap. vii. 14, 7, 9, 31, 2, 5, 6.[14, 17, 19, 31, 32, 35, 36.?] He is the model of false penitents, who are actuated by servile fear.
Free and independent, (Calmet) like Antioch. (Pliny, [Natural History?] v. 21.)

Athenians. This seems to have been put for Antiochians, chap. iv. 9., in Greek; which name would suit better here, as Epiphanes had no power over Athens. (Grotius; Calmet) --- Yet it was highly privileged (Haydock) above all the cities of Greece. (Menochius) --- Jason had obtained for the citizens of Jerusalem to be called Antiochians, chap. vi. 1. But this grant had been revoked, or not carried into effect since the late troubles. (Calmet) --- Here the privilege is to be extended to all the Jews. (Haydock) --- Ptolemais and Calliroe enjoyed the same. (Harduin.)
Sacrifices, as Darius, Philometor, and afterwards (1 Machabees x. 39.) Nicator did, 1 Esdras vi. 9. (Calmet)

Subjects. Literally, "citizens." (Haydock) --- Similar addresses (ver. 20.) were sent by the emperors to the Romans; and by Cæsar and Anthony to their allies. (Josephus, Antiquities xiv. 17., and 22.; Tull. Epist.)

Father: Antiochus the great. The Persian monarchs generally took this precaution. --- Countries. So profane authors style the provinces beyond the Euphrates [River]. Diodorus, St. Jerome (in Daniel xi.) and others, inform us that Antiochus attempted to plunder the temple of Belus, at Elymais, and took off a vast sum of money under pretext of paying the tribute to the Romans. But the neighbouring nations fell upon him, and cut him with his army to pieces. Philopator succeeded to the throne.
Antiochus Eupator, nine years old. --- Below. This is lost.
Favours. He must have been deranged. (Calmet)

Mountains, at Tabes, (Polybius) in Patacene. (Curtius v.) --- Historians relate that he lost his senses, (daimonesas) being terrified by a demon, on account of his criminal attempt against the temple of Diana. (Polybius, excerp. Vales.) (St. Jerome) --- This was a real crime in him, as he took the idol for a deity. But his conduct towards the temple and nation of the Jews would probably weigh heavier upon his conscience. (Calmet) --- St. Cyprian (exhort.) styles him "an inveterate enemy to all good; nay, in Antiochus antichrist is expressed." (Worthington)

That was. Syriac, "son of his nurse," appointed regent. --- Philometor Lysias asserted his title to the regency, and had the young king, so that Philip applied to the Egyptians to help in the execution of the last will of the deceased. (Calmet) --- Read 1 Machabees vi. 17. (Worthington)

f: Commentary on 2 Maccabees

The things that were briefly noted in the previous book about the end of Antiochus are explained more fully in this one. Mystically, however, it shows that the persecutors of Christians, for the evil deeds they have committed and the works of injustice they have performed, will in the future receive from the Lord the just recompense of punishments; and that the one who here did not fear to disturb the hearts of the faithful will, in the final vengeance, be tormented by inward pains with late repentance. Concerning this it is written in the Book of Wisdom: Then the righteous will stand with great steadfastness against those who have oppressed them and who have taken away their labors. Seeing this, they will be troubled with terrible fear, and will marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation. Groaning with anguish of spirit, they will say within themselves, as they do penance: These are the ones whom we once held in contempt and made a catch phrase of reproach. We fools considered their life madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are counted among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints. Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness has not shone for us, and the sun of understanding has not risen upon us. We have grown weary in the way of iniquity and destruction, and we have walked difficult paths, but the way of the Lord we have not known. What has our pride profited us, or what has the boasting of riches brought us? All those things have passed away like a shadow, etc. (Wisdom 5).
